 Un nouveau virus, le HMPV, submerge les hôpitaux en Chine et inquiète l'Europe : Comment le distinguer d'un simple rhume ?

Un virus saisonnier, le métapneumovirus humain (HMPV), provoque une vague d'infections en Chine, avec des répercussions signalées jusqu'en Europe. Face à des symptômes similaires à ceux du rhume, de la grippe ou même de la COVID-19, il est crucial de savoir identifier ce nouveau virus.

Des images diffusées sur les réseaux sociaux témoignent d'hôpitaux chinois débordés par l'afflux de patients. Bien qu'aucune épidémie n'ait été officiellement déclarée, les autorités sanitaires chinoises constatent une augmentation significative des syndromes pseudo-grippaux. Le HMPV représente une part non négligeable de ces infections, dépassant même des virus bien connus comme la COVID-19 et l'adénovirus, avec respectivement 6,2 % des infections respiratoires et 5,4 % des hospitalisations. Cette situation a alerté des virologues européens, notamment le Belge Marc Van Ranst.

Au Royaume-Uni, les autorités sanitaires ont tiré la sonnette d'alarme face à un doublement des cas de HMPV en seulement deux semaines. Cette recrudescence ne se limite pas à l'Europe, touchant également la Malaisie, l'Inde et le Kazakhstan. L'augmentation des cas positifs au Royaume-Uni, passant de 2,42 % début décembre à 4,5 % début janvier, pourrait même être sous-estimée.

Le HMPV se manifeste par des symptômes qui peuvent facilement être confondus avec un rhume, une grippe ou la COVID-19 : Toux, Nez bouché, Fièvre, Douleurs musculaires
, Perte de goût et d'odorat, Sensation de pression dans les oreilles et le visage, Difficulté à respirer.

Cependant, le HMPV peut entraîner des complications plus graves, en particulier chez les jeunes enfants, les personnes âgées et les personnes immunodéprimées.

HMVP refers to "Human Metapneumovirus" (HMPV), which is a respiratory virus that can cause respiratory infections in humans. The virus was first identified in 2001, and generally infects children, the elderly, and individuals with weakened immune systems.

In more serious cases, especially in infants, the elderly, or individuals with chronic respiratory diseases, HMPV can cause bronchiolitis (inflammation of the small airways in the lungs) or pneumonia.
HMPV is spread through droplets released when coughing or sneezing, similar to how the flu and COVID-19 viruses spread. It can also be spread through direct contact with contaminated surfaces.

There is no specific vaccine for HMPV. To prevent transmission, the following steps can be taken:
- Wash your hands regularly with soap and water for at least 20 seconds.
- Avoid contact with people who are sick, especially if symptoms include coughing or runny nose.

- Get enough rest
- Drink plenty of water
- Fever and cough relievers.
- Supplemental oxygen if needed.
In general, HMPV infections can heal on their own within a few days to weeks. However, in more severe cases, medical treatment or hospitalization may be required.

Treatment and Prevention:
Currently, there are no specific antiviral treatments or vaccines available for HMPV. Management of the infection is largely

supportive, focusing on symptom relief. However, research into antivirals like favipiravir suggests potential efficacy against HMPV, although it is not yet clear if it will become a standard treatment.

Research Developments:
There is ongoing research into understanding the molecular interactions between antivirals and RNA viruses like HMPV. Studies are analyzing how drugs like favipiravir interact with the RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp) of HMPV, which could lead to new

therapeutic approaches. However, these findings are preliminary and require further investigation.

2/
HMPV has a negative-sense RNA genome encoding 9 proteins.

Key players:
•Fusion protein (F): Mediates viral entry.
•N protein: Protects viral RNA.
•M2-2 protein: Suppresses immune responses, promoting re-infection.

HMPV binds heparan sulfate receptors for host cell entry.

4/ Pathogenesis
Persistent infection = weak immune response & impaired T-cell function.

HMPV disrupts dendritic cells, reducing CD4+ T-cell activity.
Emerging evidence suggests systemic spread (e.g., brain & ear infections).

5/ Diagnosis

RT-PCR = Gold standard (100% sensitivity, 96% specificity).

Other methods: ELISA, immunofluorescence, and cell cultures.

Challenges: HMPV grows slowly, delaying diagnosis.

Human metapneumovirus (HMPV) can cause respiratory disease.
HMPV spreads from person to person or surfaces to person.
Symptoms include cough, fever, nasal congestion, and shortness of breath.
Treatment is symptomatic & routine prevention strategies need to be followed.

In international collaborative studies in acute respiratory illnesses, we have documented HMPV infections from 2010 onward. HMPV has been circulating in  our community during winters, for at least 15 years. Unlike COVID this has implications on presentation and treatment.

**HMPV : Augmentation des cas en Chine et aux États-Unis – La prévention avant tout**

Le métapneumovirus humain (HMPV) attire l’attention des autorités sanitaires internationales, avec une augmentation significative des cas en Chine et une hausse préoccupante aux États-Unis. Ce virus respiratoire, souvent sous-estimé, représente une menace particulière pour les jeunes enfants, les personnes âgées et les individus immunodéprimés.

Adopter des mesures préventives est essentiel pour se protéger et limiter la propagation.

Qu’est-ce que le HMPV ?

Le HMPV est un virus respiratoire provoquant des symptômes similaires à un rhume ou une grippe, mais pouvant, dans certains cas, entraîner des complications graves telles que la pneumonie ou la bronchiolite.
•Groupes à risque :
•Jeunes enfants
•Personnes âgées
•Personnes atteintes de maladies chroniques ou avec un système immunitaire affaibli

Symptômes à reconnaître
•Fièvre
•Toux persistante
•Congestion nasale
•Difficultés respiratoires

Si les symptômes s’aggravent ou persistent, il est essentiel de consulter un médecin rapidement.

La prévention est la meilleure défense

Bien qu’il n’existe pas de vaccin pour le HMPV, des actions concrètes peuvent être mises en place pour vous protéger, vous et vos proches :
1.Lavage fréquent des mains : Utilisez de l’eau et du savon pendant au moins 20 secondes ou un désinfectant à base d’alcool.
2.Évitez le contact avec des personnes malades : Si quelqu’un présente des symptômes grippaux ou respiratoires, maintenez une distance de sécurité.
3.Couvrez le nez et la bouche : Utilisez un mouchoir ou votre coude lorsque vous toussez ou éternuez pour éviter de propager le virus.
4.Désinfectez les surfaces : Nettoyez régulièrement les surfaces et objets fréquemment touchés, comme les téléphones, poignées de porte et jouets.
5.Renforcez votre système immunitaire : Adoptez une alimentation équilibrée, dormez suffisamment et pratiquez une activité physique régulière.

Le rôle du CDC et de la collaboration internationale

Les Centres pour le contrôle et la prévention des maladies (CDC) et les autorités sanitaires mondiales surveillent de près la propagation du virus afin de prévenir des flambées plus importantes. La collaboration entre les pays sera essentielle pour identifier et contenir rapidement les nouveaux cas.

Un appel à la responsabilité individuelle
•Protégez les plus vulnérables : Les enfants et les personnes âgées sont les plus à risque ; il est crucial de tout faire pour éviter de les exposer au virus.
•Consultez un médecin en cas de symptômes suspects : Un diagnostic précoce peut prévenir des complications.
•Diffusez des informations correctes : La sensibilisation est la première étape vers la prévention.

La prévention n’est jamais prématurée. Se protéger, c’est aussi protéger son entourage.

HMPV primarily causes localised outbreaks of resp illnesses.
HMPV Enters the respiratory tract,infects the epithelial cells in the respiratory mucosa and causes inflammation and swelling of the airways.
In infants and young childrens can also leads to hypoxia.

So HMPV can lead to severe disease in the population but generally not as transmissible or severe as SARS-COV-2.

Cough
Nasal congestion
Fever
Shortness of breath
Sore throat
Wheezing (in severe cases)
Transmission
Spread through respiratory droplets when an infected person coughs or sneezes
Close contact with an infected person or touching contaminated surfaces

@RishikaSadam Human metapneumovirus (HMPV) is a respiratory virus that typically causes symptoms similar to the common cold. It belongs to the Pneumoviridae family, which also includes the respiratory syncytial virus (RSV).

@RishikaSadam Symptoms: Common symptoms of HMPV infection include:

Cough
Fever
Runny or stuffy nose
Sore throat
Wheezing
Shortness of breath
Rash

@RishikaSadam In most cases, these symptoms are mild and resolve within a few days to a week. However, HMPV can lead to more severe respiratory illnesses, such as bronchiolitis or pneumonia, especially in young children, older adults, and individuals with weakened immune systems.

@RishikaSadam Transmission: HMPV spreads through direct contact with respiratory secretions from an infected person, such as through coughing and sneezing, or by touching contaminated surfaces and then touching the face. The virus is most prevalent during late winter and early spring

@RishikaSadam Diagnosis and Treatment: Healthcare providers may diagnose HMPV based on symptoms and health history. Laboratory tests, such as PCR (polymerase chain reaction) tests, can confirm the presence of the virus. There is no specific antiviral treatment for HMPV;

🧵Understanding HMPV (Human Metapneumovirus)

1/5 🦠 What is HMPV?
HMPV is a common respiratory virus that primarily affects the lungs & airways. It was first identified in 2001 & is similar to Respiratory Syncytial Virus. It spreads through droplets, surfaces, & close contact. https://t.co/K6XKJTOOii

3/5 ⚠️ Symptoms of HMPV:

 👉🏻Cough
 👉🏻Runny nose
 👉🏻Sore throat
 👉🏻Fever
 👉🏻Wheezing or difficulty breathing in severe cases

Symptoms often resemble the flu or a cold, making it easy to overlook.

2/5 🤒 Who is at risk?
HMPV can affect people of all ages, but:

 👉🏻Young children
 👉🏻Older adults
 👉🏻Immunocompromised individuals
are more likely to experience severe symptoms.

4/5 🩺 How is it treated?
There’s no specific antiviral treatment for HMPV. Care is supportive:

 👉🏻Rest
 👉🏻Fluids
 👉🏻Fever reducers (if necessary)
 👉🏻In severe cases, hospitalization for oxygen therapy or other interventions may be required.

5/5 🛡️ Prevention is key!

 👉🏻Wash your hands frequently
 👉🏻Avoid touching your face
 👉🏻Stay home when sick
 👉🏻Clean surfaces regularly
 👉🏻Wear a mask if asymptomatic

HMPV is seasonal (winter/spring). Stay informed to protect yourself and others!

HMPV causes flu-like symptoms and can lead to severe respiratory issues, It affects individuals across all age groups, with young children, the elderly, and those with compromised immune systems .

What is HMPV

HMPV belongs to the Pneumoviridae family, the same family as respiratory syncytial virus (RSV). It typically causes upper and lower respiratory infections, presenting symptoms similar to a common cold or flu.

Symptoms of HMPV

🔸cough and runny nose, 
🔸fever, 
🔸sore throat, 
🔸wheezing
🔸shortness of breath in severe cases.

How does HMPV spread?
HMPV spreads through droplets from coughing or sneezing, close contact such as touching or shaking hands, contaminated surfaces, followed by touching the mouth, nose or eyes

While HMPV is driving a rise in respiratory infections, it is neither a new virus nor a looming pandemic threat. Seasonal spikes are expected, particularly as people reacclimate to common pathogens after Covid-19 lockdowns.

HMPV typically clears up within a week, but it’s important for young children, older adults, and those with existing health conditions to stay cautious. Following preventive measures can reduce the risk of infections.
There is no specific antiviral treatment or vaccine for HMPV as of now. Treatment include symptomatic treatment. Most important preventive measures include handwashing, and staying home when sick.

2/ What is HMPV?
HMPV is a respiratory virus first identified in 2001. It primarily infects the lungs and airways, leading to symptoms like coughing, fever, shortness of breath, and fatigue. Think of it as RSV’s lesser-known cousin

3/ Who is at risk?
While it can affect anyone, HMPV is particularly dangerous for:

Infants and young children
Elderly individuals
People with weakened immune systems or chronic lung conditions

5/ How does it spread?
HMPV spreads through respiratory droplets (sneezing, coughing) and by touching contaminated surfaces. It’s highly contagious, especially in crowded areas like schools, offices, or public transport

6/ Is there a cure?
No specific antiviral treatment or vaccine exists for HMPV yet. Management focuses on relieving symptoms: staying hydrated, using over-the-counter medications, and seeking medical care for severe cases.

7/ Why is this concerning?
The first HMPV case in India signals potential for outbreaks, especially during flu season when other respiratory viruses are already in circulation. Monitoring and early detection are crucial.

Symptoms of HMPV

1. Fever 🤒
2. Cough 🤧
3. Shortness of breath
4. Runny nose
5. Fatigue 😴
Severe cases may lead to bronchitis or pneumonia, requiring medical attention.

What is HMPV?

Discovered in 2001, HMPV is a respiratory virus from the same family as RSV (Respiratory Syncytial Virus). It spreads via:

- Droplets from coughing/sneezing.
- Contaminated surfaces.
- Close contact.
It’s more common than you think!

Who is at risk?

While anyone can catch HMPV, it’s more severe in:
- Children under 5.
- Older adults.
- Those with weakened immune systems or chronic illnesses.
Symptoms often mimic the flu, but complications can arise in vulnerable groups.

Currently, there’s no specific vaccine or treatment for HMPV. Supportive care is key.

What Is HMPV?
Human metapneumovirus (HMPV) is a virus that can cause flu-like illness in people of all ages, although some people are more at risk, including young children, older adults and people with weakened immune systems.

How does HMPV spread?

Like other similar viruses, HMPV usually spreads from person to person through droplets from coughing and sneezing, through human contact such as hugging or kissing, and through touching surfaces and objects contaminated with the virus

What Are the Symptoms of HMPV?
HMPV symptoms are similar to other flu-like diseases, including coughing, a fever and a stuffy or runny nose.
In some cases, sick people may experience a shortness of breath and this can progress to bronchitis

What is Human Metapneumovirus (HMPV)?
HMPV is a respiratory virus that causes illnesses ranging from mild cold-like symptoms to severe respiratory infections, particularly in young children, the elderly, and people with weakened immune systems.

Symptoms of HMPV:
•Fever
•Cough
•Shortness of breath
•Nasal congestion
•Sore throat
•Wheezing
In severe cases, it can lead to bronchiolitis or pneumonia.

How does HMPV spread?
HMPV spreads through:
•Direct contact (shaking hands, touching an infected person).
•Respiratory droplets from coughing or sneezing.
•Touching contaminated surfaces and then touching your face (mouth, nose, or eyes).

Human Metapneumo Virus,HMPV is a type of virus that was identified 2001 in Netherland. It affects the respiratory system.

It belongs to the Pneumoviridae family, which als includes RSV, Respiratory Syncytial Virus.

HMPV is highly contagious and can be spread through direct contact with an infected person, cough and sneezing.

HMPV can cause coughing, sneezing, running nose, wheezing,and shortness of breath.

Symptoms last for 7-10 days.

HMPV can be diagnosed using molecular test such as PCR, polymerase chain reaction.

There is no specific treatment for HMPV. Symptoms can be managed, rest, fluids, Over the Counter Medication oxygen therapy if case is worst.

Prevention for  HMPV for now are good hygiene, avoid close distance, stay home when sick

Human metapneumovirus (hMPV) is a respiratory virus that was first identified in 2001. It's part of the Paramyxoviridae family, which includes other viruses like RSV (Respiratory Syncytial Virus) and parainfluenza.

Diagnosis:
hMPV can be confirmed through laboratory tests, such as PCR testing, though it’s often not specifically tested unless symptoms are severe or the patient is hospitalized.

Treatment:
There's no specific antiviral treatment for hMPV. Care is supportive:

Rest

Hydration

Fever reducers (e.g., acetaminophen or ibuprofen)
In severe cases, oxygen therapy or hospitalization may be required.

Elle touche particulièrement les enfants – même les nourrissons ne sont pas protégés contre la maladie.

Les touristes soupçonnent qu'ils sont porteurs du métapneumovirus (HMPV). Leur état est si grave que les Russes sont prêts à être traités avec n'importe quoi - aussi bien des médicaments locaux que des décoctions à base de plantes.

Elle touche le plus souvent les enfants de moins de 14 ans dans les provinces du nord du pays. Le ministère chinois de la Santé n'a introduit aucune restriction, mais le département russe a pris le contrôle de la situation.

HMPV is a common respiratory virus, especially affecting children, causing flu-like symptoms.
While HMPV isn't new, the recent surge has overwhelmed hospitals in China, particularly children's hospitals. This has led to concerns and increased scrutiny of the situation.
(2/5)

HMPV spreads through respiratory droplets, similar to how COVID-19 spreads. Symptoms include cough, fever, nasal congestion, and sore throat. In some cases, it can lead to more severe respiratory infections.
(3/5)

There's no specific antiviral treatment or vaccine for HMPV. Treatment focuses on managing symptoms. The Chinese government is closely monitoring the situation and taking steps to address the outbreak.

Human Metapneumovirus (HMPV) is a respiratory virus that belongs to the Pneumoviridae family, similar to the respiratory syncytial virus (RSV). Here are some key points about HMPV:

Symptoms: HMPV typically causes symptoms similar to those of the common cold, including cough, fever, nasal congestion, sore throat, and shortness of breath. In severe cases, it can lead to bronchitis or pneumonia, particularly in young children, older adults, and individuals
Seasonality: HMPV is more active during the late winter and early spring, similar to the seasonal pattern of RSV and influenza

Risk Groups: While anyone can contract HMPV, it poses a higher risk to children under 5, adults over 65, and those with compromised immune systems or chronic respiratory conditions like asthma or COPD.
Prevention: There is no vaccine for HMPV. Preventive measures include regular hand washing, avoiding close contact with sick individuals, and cleaning frequently touched surfaces.

HMPV (Human Metapneumovirus) is a respiratory virus that primarily affects the lungs and airways. It was first discovered in 2001 and is part of the Metapneumovirus genus in the Paramyxoviridae family, which also includes other viruses like the respiratory syncytial virus (RSV).

Treatment:
- There is no specific antiviral treatment for HMPV.
- Treatment is generally supportive, focusing on alleviating symptoms like fever and congestion.
- In severe cases, hospitalization may be required, especially for oxygen therapy or mechanical ventilation.

Prevention:
- Like other respiratory viruses, good hygiene practices, such as frequent hand washing and avoiding close contact with infected individuals, are crucial for preventing the spread of HMPV.
- There is no vaccine currently available for HMPV.

Transmission:
- HMPV spreads through respiratory droplets when an infected person coughs, sneezes, or talks.
- It can also spread by touching surfaces contaminated with the virus and then touching the face.

What is HMPV?

Discovered: 2001 in the Netherlands, but has circulated globally for decades.

Virus Family: Related to RSV (Respiratory Syncytial Virus).

Symptoms: Flu-like (cough, fever, nasal congestion). Severe cases can cause pneumonia or bronchitis.
Unlike COVID-19, HMPV doesn’t spread as aggressively or cause mass hospitalizations.

Pandemic Potential?

Unlikely: HMPV has been around for decades, and most people have immunity from prior infections.

Experts see no evidence of a global emergency.

Almost every child gets HMPV by age 5, with reinfections common but usually mild.

HMPV is serious for vulnerable populations, but it’s not a new or global crisis. Stay informed and take basic precautions to protect yourself and others.
